grammar.name: Pronunciation
grammar.wording: How Celan sounds in the mouth: vowels, consonants, and the flow of euphony.

grammar.name: Sentence Shape: How Celan Moves
grammar.wording: How Celan moves through action, questions, commands, negation, and conditions.
grammar.examples:
Plain VSO Sentence: `var I an dren.` (I go to the water.)
Question: `ra var ser?` (Where does the friend go?)
Negative Question: `ra ver var ser?` (Does the friend not go?)
Command: `va var dren!` (Go to the water!)
Conditional Pair: `rath var ser, nor-var I an dren.` (If the friend goes, I will go to the water.)

grammar.name: Word Building: How Celan Grows Words
grammar.wording: How roots, compounds, suffixes, and sound-shaping grow Celan words from core ideas.
grammar.examples:
One Clean Compound: `Morldren` (Waterfall) (Built from `Morl` / Mountain + `Dren` / Water)
One Suffix-Based Derivation: `Shalaen` (To see) (Built from `Shal` / Light + `-aen` / action suffix)
One Plural Form: `Serin` (Friends) (Built from `Ser` / Friend + `-in` / plural suffix)
One `-eth` Form: `Woreth` (Full / Abundant) (Built from `Wor` / Abundance + `-eth` / having the quality of)
One "Same Idea, Different Build" Contrast: To say Dynamic Equilibrium (balancing a fierce, fiery energy):
A tough Valkeldorian warrior builds it harsh: `Krezthal`.
A poetic Jasaran philosopher builds it smooth: `Krezathal`.

grammar.name: Possession and Relation
grammar.wording: Distinguish ownership, personal possession, relational bonds, and absence.
grammar.examples:
rinaen aiv an doran-ian. — There is pain in my torso.
drenselaen I noka-ian. — I wash my vulva.
drenaen La dren kora rinaen La-ka kelvor kadreneth. — They drink water because their mouth is dry.

grammar.name: Number and Measure: How Celan Counts the World
grammar.wording: How Celan builds numbers, scales them upward, handles subtraction, and expresses quantity without articles.
grammar.examples:
Base List: `verin`, `unar`, `del`, `tren`... (0, 1, 2, 3...).
One Teen Form: `tenar unar` (11 — built by combining 10 and 1).
One Tens Form: `Ten-del` (20 — built as Two tens).
One Hundreds Form: `Hek-quen` (400 — built as Four hundreds).
One Additive Example: `Ten-del peth` (25 — Twenty plus five).
One Subtraction Example: `Hek-quen Ven Hek-del` (400 minus 200 = 200).

grammar.name: Gender, Address, and Social Use: How Celan Connects People
grammar.wording: How Celan handles identity, respect, address, and social nuance through form choice.
grammar.examples:
One Direct Respectful Address: `var I dren, Li-Ser.` (I go to the water, respected friend).
One Gender-Term Usage Example: `Azon` (A feminine man — showing the fluidity of combining the `Azan` feminine essence with a male subject).
One Cultural/Register Contrast: Formal: `aen` (to speak deep truths) vs. Informal: `kel` (to casually chat).
One Poetic/Socially Elevated Phrasing Example: `vael vaar an shara-ya.` (May peace be on your path — using the poetic wish particle `vael` to offer a gentle, elevated blessing).

grammar.name: Writing Conventions: How Celan Appears on the Page
grammar.wording: How Celan uses lowercase, capitals, reverence, and emphasis to make meaning visible on the page.
grammar.examples:
One Normal Lowercase Sentence: `var kadron an morl.` (The man goes to the mountain — entirely lowercase because no specific names or grand concepts are used).
One Sentence with `I`: `var I an dren.` (I go to the water — the verb `var` is lowercase, but the `I` stands tall).
One Sacred/Archetypal Contrast: `terra` (mundane soil/dirt) vs. `Terra` (the mystical Heart of the world).
Ordinary sentence opening: `ohmaen I Ya.` (I love you.)
Poetic: `rinaen I an Thar-ka.` (I am Desire itself — elevating personal desire into a grand, archetypal force).

grammar.name: Cultural Voice: How Ohnosha Speaks Celan Differently
grammar.wording: How one universal tongue takes on different national voices across Ohnosha.
grammar.examples:
Verdalrisian: `lorin shara ya an Kinnmor, Li-Ser?` (Where does your path guide you this morning, Respected-Friend?)
Pelagaean: `ra shalil ya, Ser?` (Where do you flow, Friend?)
Zarithan: `ra min ya, Ser?` (Where are you headed, Friend?)
Valkeldorian: `aen shara-ya, Ser!` (State your path, Friend!)
Mechuman: `aen ya varash, Ser.` (State your destination, Friend.)
Nivveilian: `an eshreth, ra var ya, Ser?` (In this hazy sky, where are you going, Friend?)
Jasaran: `shal lorin shara-ya an nor-ka, Ser?` (Does the light guide your path in this moment, Friend?)
Marakorian: `ra rinaen shara-ya lian, Li-Ser?` (Is your path a proper one, Respected-Friend?)

grammar.name: The Phonetics of Celan: Clarity, Flow, and Euphony
grammar.wording:
Celan balances the firmness of its structure with the smooth flow of its breath.
Its sound system depends on clear vowels, supportive consonants, and euphonic smoothing when a compound grows too harsh.

grammar.name: Numbers and Basic Math
grammar.wording:
Celan starts with a base set of number words, then builds upward with prefixes for tens, hundreds, thousands, and beyond.
Addition is usually shown by additive number building, while subtraction uses the marker Ven between number forms.
grammar.examples:
Base numbers: Verin (0), Unar (1), Del (2), Tren (3), Quen (4), Peth (5), Senar (6), Sethe (7), Oven (8), Nevar (9), Tenar (10)
Tens: Ten-del = 20
Mixed number: Tenar unar = 11
Hundreds: Hek-unar = 100
Thousands: Mel-unar = 1,000
Ten-thousands: Fen-unar = 10,000
Hundred-thousands: Hek-Mel-unar = 100,000
Addition: Hek-quen Ten-peth = 450 (400 + 50)
Subtraction: Hek-quen Ven Hek-del = 400 - 200 = 200

grammar.name: The Architecture of Relation: Prepositions, Place, and Time
grammar.wording:
Because Celan relies on a strict Verb-Subject-Object flow, prepositions do immense structural work.
They act as the architectural joints of a sentence, defining movement, accompaniment, absence, elevation, location, and temporal setting.

grammar.name: Action-First Sentence Structure
grammar.wording:
Celan primarily follows Verb-Subject-Object (VSO) order.
This action-first structure reflects a worldview that foregrounds movement, relation, and what is being done before who is doing it.

grammar.name: Questions and Commands
grammar.wording:
Start ordinary questions with ra.
For a negative question, place Ver before the verb.
For a direct command, start the sentence with va.
grammar.examples:
ra var ser an dren? — "Does the friend go to the water?"
ra ver var ser an dren? — "Does the friend not go to the water?"
va var an dren! — "Go to the water!"

grammar.name: Capitalization and Emphasis
grammar.wording:
Celan normally begins sentences with lowercase unless the opening word already qualifies for capitalization.
Capitals are used for archetypal concepts, names, nations, specific titles, the pronoun I, and sometimes for poetic or emotional emphasis.
grammar.examples:
Sentence start: var I an dren. (not Var I an dren.)
Archetypal concepts: Terra vs. terra; Dral vs. dral; Rathor vs. rathor
Names and titles: Velmarin; Eh'lara; Ka'tharyn
Pronoun I: I
Capitalization examples: Ordinary "ohmaen I Ya." / Poetic "Rinaen I an Thar-ka."

grammar.name: Personal Pronouns
grammar.wording: Celan distinguishes between first, second, and third persons, with singular and plural forms.
grammar.examples:
1st Person Singular: I — Remains simple and universal.
1st Person Plural: Ilin — Represents "we" as a group bound by common purpose.
2nd Person Singular: Ya — A straightforward pronoun for “you.”
2nd Person Plural: Yalin — "You all." Signifies a collective of individuals addressed.
3rd Person Singular: La — Neutral pronoun meaning “he/she/they.”
3rd Person Plural: Lalin — Means “they” (a group not including speaker or addressee).

grammar.name: Relational and Poetic Focus
grammar.wording: Celan terms prioritize relationships and qualities over rigid definitions. For example:
grammar.examples:
tal theon thal an Ilin. — The neutral person gives balance to us.
nethaen azon an nethor. — The feminine man rests on the seat.

grammar.name: Contextual Flexibility
grammar.wording:
These terms can describe identities in various ways:
● Default Use: Standalone nouns (e.g., Kadron, Azron, Theon).
● Descriptive Use: Combine with other terms for clarity or depth.
grammar.examples: nethaen azon an nethor. — The feminine man rests on the seat.

grammar.name: Cultural Variations
grammar.wording:
Each Ohnoshan culture may adapt these terms to fit their values:
● Pelagae: Emphasizes fluidity and uses Azon frequently for spiritual men.
● Nivveil: Highlights balance, favoring Thee-based descriptors.
● Valkeldor: Values strength and may use Kadon to honor warrior women.

grammar.name: Gender-Neutral Address
grammar.wording: Use Thee terms for inclusivity in formal or neutral contexts:
grammar.examples: tal theon thal an Ilin. — The neutral person gives balance to us.

grammar.name: Combining Qualities
grammar.wording: Layer terms to reflect specific traits:
grammar.examples:
● Kadron-Azon: A man with both masculine and feminine qualities.
● Azron-Theon: A woman embodying neutrality and balance.

grammar.name: Tenses and Aspects
grammar.wording: Celan verbs do not conjugate based on tense. Instead, tenses are indicated by prefixes and suffixes.
grammar.examples:
Present: var I dren. / I go to the water.
Past: tha-var I dren. / I went to the water.
Future: nor-var I dren. / I will go to the water.
Continuous: varal I dren. / I am going to the water.
Perfective: varath I dren. / I have gone to the water.
Habitual: varas I dren. / I usually go to the water.
Also attested with explicit destination: var I an dren. The bare goal is attested for var; do not generalize it to every motion verb.

grammar.name: Negation
grammar.wording:
Negation is formed by placing Ver before the verb or noun.
● Verb Negation: Ver before the verb negates it.
● Noun Negation: Ver before a noun negates its existence.
grammar.examples: ver var I dren. — I do not go to the water.

grammar.name: Conditionals
grammar.wording:
● Conditional “If”: Use Rath to introduce conditions.
● Hypothetical Future: Combine Rath with future tense.
● Contrary-to-Fact: Use past tense markers.
grammar.examples:
rath var ser, var I dren. — If the friend goes, I go to the water.
rath nor-var ser, nor-var I dren. — If the friend will go, I will go to the water.

grammar.name: Pluralization
grammar.wording:
Rule:
● -in is added to nouns ending in consonants.
● -n is added to nouns ending in vowels.
grammar.examples:
● Ser (friend) → Serin (friends)
● Thar (heart) → Tharin (hearts)
● Esh (sky) → Eshin (skies)
● Dren (water) → Drenin (waters)
● Tera (home) → Teran (homes)

grammar.name: Derivation and Word Formation
grammar.wording:
Suffixes:
● -or: Place/Location
● -en: Honorific/Respected form
● -lin: Collective/Diminutive
● -aen: Verb-forming
Prefixes:
● Tha-: Past tense
● Nor-: Future tense
● Ver-: Negation
● Li-: Respect/Honorific
grammar.examples:
● -or: Place/Location / Shal + or = Shalor (sanctuary/light place)
● -en: Honorific/Respected form / Liorin + en = Liorinen (honored elder/teacher)
● -lin: Collective/Diminutive / Elin = child; Ilin = we
● -aen: Verb-forming / Lian (truth) → Lianaen (to speak truth)
● Tha-: Past tense
● Nor-: Future tense
● Ver-: Negation
● Li-: Respect/Honorific

grammar.name: Compounding
grammar.wording:
Rule:
● Primary root comes first, refining the meaning with the second root.
grammar.examples:
● Terra + Dren = Terradren (fertile soil/well-irrigated land)
● Dren + Shal = Drenshal (reflective pool/crystal-clear spring)
● Morl + Dren = Morldren (waterfall/mountain stream)
● Terra + Esh = Terraesh (horizon/place where earth meets sky)
● Krez + or = Krezor (forge)

grammar.name: Articles (Definite/Indefinite)
grammar.wording: Decision: Confirming Celan generally lacks specific articles like "the" or "a/an". Definiteness and indefiniteness are primarily determined by context, word order (VSO often places known info earlier), or specific demonstratives if needed (though none explicitly listed, could be developed).

grammar.name: Quantifiers
grammar.wording: Quantifiers are placed before the noun they modify.
grammar.examples: Ilinor; Som; Melen; Felin; Ekor

grammar.name: Levels of Politeness
grammar.wording:
1. Casual/Familiar:
○ Use plain pronouns and address by name or role without modifiers.
2. Respectful/Polite:
○ Add Li- prefix to show respect.
3. Honorific/Formal-High Respect:
○ Use both Li- and -en suffix.
grammar.examples:
var I dren, Ser. — I go to the water, friend.
var I dren, Li-Ser. — I go to the water, respected friend.
var Li-Ya dren. — You, respected one, go to the water.

grammar.name: Relative Clauses
grammar.wording:
Relative Pronoun: Lior (who/which)
Structure:
● Noun + Lior + Clause
grammar.examples:
Ser Lior var an dren. — The friend who goes to the water.
var I an terra ser Ser Lior var an dren. — I go home with the friend who goes to the water.

grammar.name: Comparatives and Superlatives
grammar.wording:
Comparatives:
● Ther (more than)
Structure:
● X Adjective Ther Y
Superlatives:
● Thaal (most)
Structure:
● X Adjective Thaal
grammar.examples:
rinaen dren-ian shaleth ther La-ka dren. — My water is brighter than their water.
rinaen dren-ian shaleth thaal. — My water is brightest.
rinaen dren-ian shaleth thaal morldren. — My water is brightest of mountain waters.

grammar.name: Conditionals
grammar.wording:
Conditional Marker: Rath (if)
Structure:
● Rath + Clause + Main Clause
grammar.examples:
rath var Ya dren, nor-var I dren. — If you go to the water, I will go to the water.
rath tha-var Ya an dren, tha-talaen I emil. — If you had gone to the water, I would have gotten food.

grammar.name: The Adjectival Suffix -eth
grammar.wording: The suffix -eth, previously observed in ceremonial nouns (e.g., Shal'taleth) and the comparative adjective shaleth (brighter), is now formally established as one of Celan's most important derivational suffixes. It serves a dual function, creating both adjectives and abstract ritual nouns from a single root.
grammar.examples:
Adjectival: Shal → Shaleth; Wor → Woreth; Gorm → Gormeth; Kal → Kaleth
Nominal/Ritual: Shal'taleth; Aen'Moreth

grammar.name: Verb Mood and Modality
grammar.wording: To express concepts of ability, necessity, and desire, Celan employs a system of modal adverbs placed after the subject in a VSO sentence.
grammar.examples: Ability: Lianeth; Necessity: Belshara; Possibility: Rethlian; Desire: Thar-ka

grammar.name: Subjunctive Mood
grammar.wording: Rule: Place the particle vael at the beginning of a clause to express wishes, hopes, suggestions, or conditions that are not currently real.
grammar.examples:
Vael vaar an shara-ya. (May peace be on your path.)
Vael rinaen I an eshlin, varal I an esh. (If I were a bird, I would be going to the sky.)
Vael aen Ya. (May you speak / Please speak.)

grammar.name: Passive Voice: nor-ka
grammar.wording: Celan expresses the passive voice not by modifying the verb, but by re-contextualizing the object as the "echo" or "wake" of a completed action whose agent is unknown or unimportant.
grammar.examples:
Active: pralaen Azron belkor. — The woman makes the tunic.
Passive: pralaen belkor an Azron nor-ka. — The tunic was made by the woman.

grammar.name: Advanced Pronouns: Dual Number and Clusivity
grammar.wording: The Celan pronoun system is expanded with the Dual Number and Clusivity. Dual pronouns replace plural counterparts when the group consists of exactly two entities. Use Ilin when including the listener; use Imen when referring to your group to an outsider.
grammar.examples: Inko; Yako; Lako; Ilin; Imen

grammar.name: Essential Conjunctions
grammar.wording: Conjunctions are the grammatical glue that connects words, phrases, and clauses. Ser is re-purposed from Ser (With) as And. Reth is re-purposed from Reth (Uncertainty) as Or.
grammar.examples: Rinaen morlak ser dren. / Ra drenaen Ya dren reth phelvin?

grammar.name: Optional content-question tails
grammar.wording: Standard questions begin with ra. In a content question a speaker may close the clause with mu what nu when zhe why sha how lo where or ri who to name the missing answer category. The closing particle is grammatically correct but optional. Without it context may supply the intended answer type. Ri does not distinguish English who from whom.
grammar.examples: ra var ser? / Where does the friend go? Context supplies place. / ra var ser lo? / Where does the friend go? Lo makes place explicit.

grammar.name: Question Frame as open gap and missing anchor
grammar.wording: In the optional Question Frame ra opens an unresolved thought the clause establishes what is known and the final content particle identifies the missing anchor that would complete the thought. This interpretation describes a practical Ohnoshan habit of inquiry and does not make the explicit closing particle mandatory.
grammar.examples: ra + known clause + mu/nu/zhe/sha/lo/ri? / The answer supplies the named missing matter time cause method place or identity.

grammar.name: Possession: spacing and suffix hierarchy
grammar.wording: Standalone ka is exclusively without or no. Possessive -ka must be hyphenated to the possessor. Body parts, inner states, personal clothes, and primary personal gear use post-nominal -ian (my), -ya (your), or -eshen (his/her/their). Collective, titled, compound, and other third-person possessors use possessor-ka. The user explicitly permits La-ka kelvor for their mouth, including this third-person body-part construction. -ian never means their. Relational -esh indicates a bond; it does not by itself specify a third-person owner.
grammar.examples:
I-ka dren — My water.
Ilin-ka emil — Our meal.
rinaen aiv an doran-ian. — There is pain in my torso.
drenselaen I noka-ian. — I wash my vulva.
La-ka kelvor — Their mouth.
Var I ka shal. — I go without light.

grammar.name: Two permitted orders for a governing verb and its complement
grammar.wording: Both V1 + Subject + V2 + Object and V1 + V2 + Subject + Object are permitted. The first places the subject directly after the governing verb; the second presents the combined action before the subject.
grammar.examples:
siv I pralaen krezor. — I try to make the hearth.
siv gavaen I zor. — I try to hunt the animal.
sivrethaen belnoraen rakumek nor mekreth. — The computers fail to synchronize during the system malfunction.

grammar.name: Varan and the universal continuous suffix
grammar.wording: -al remains the universal continuous suffix. Varan is the lexicalized locative-stative form Var + An: to reside, stay, or be located at a physical place. It does not establish continuous -an. An supplies physical location; Nor supplies time.
grammar.examples:
varal I dren. — I am going to the water.
varan I an Varthas. — I am residing in the city.
nor-var I an Varthas. — I will go to the city.

grammar.name: Plural and participant senses of -in
grammar.wording: The existing plural rule remains: consonant-final nouns take -in; vowel-final nouns take -n. Separately, -in has an approved person/participant sense connecting a person or group to a bond, place, or category. That sense does not replace ordinary plurals.
grammar.examples:
nderun — testicles.
welrinin — citizens.
Shalor-in — one belonging to the sanctuary.

grammar.examples: Kalvok; Kalrath; Rethlian — Clan / Apex Predator / Might [PE-S1-0009]

grammar.wording: These are teaching illustrations, not ordinary sentence examples.
grammar.examples:
